slots.practicalActivity: Sketch an account/database/schema namespace for a hypothetical retail company with a raw_customer database and a governance database, then draw a small role hierarchy (3-4 roles) showing which role inherits from which, ending in a single top role like SYSADMIN. Write one sentence naming which role should own objects created in the governance database.
slots.deliverable: A sketched database/schema namespace plus a 3-4 role hierarchy diagram with an ownership decision.

slots.practicalActivity: Write the GRANT statements needed to let a role named analytics_reader select from one table in raw_customer, including any usage grants on the database and schema the role needs first. Then review your statements against the lesson's best practices (least privilege, granting to roles not users, avoiding direct ACCOUNTADMIN use) and note one change you'd make.
slots.deliverable: A complete usage-plus-select GRANT chain for one role, plus one written best-practice correction applied to it.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a CREATE MASKING POLICY for a STRING column that fully masks the value for every role except ACCOUNTADMIN, and a second policy for a DATE column that returns NULL for everyone except ACCOUNTADMIN. Then sketch a mapping table with at least two role/value pairs (e.g. role, city) and write the CREATE ROW ACCESS POLICY that checks it via EXISTS, including an admin bypass clause.
slots.deliverable: Two masking policies (STRING and DATE) plus one row access policy backed by a mapping table, all with correct RETURNS types.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a CREATE SECURE VIEW wrapping one masked table from the previous slot, and explain in one sentence why a secure view's definition is hidden from SHOW VIEWS and GET_DDL for non-owners. Then rewrite your masking policy from the previous slot to check a column tag (via SYSTEM$GET_TAG_ON_CURRENT_COLUMN) instead of being hardcoded to one column, and apply it to a tag with ALTER TAG ... SET MASKING POLICY.
slots.deliverable: One CREATE SECURE VIEW statement with its confidentiality rationale, plus one tag-aware masking policy wired to a tag via ALTER TAG.

slots.practicalActivity: Data protection lab: on a test table of your choosing (or one you create in a trial Snowflake account), attach both a masking policy on a STRING column and a row access policy on a region-style column at the same time. Query the table as a low-privileged role and confirm both controls apply simultaneously and independently -- masked values and filtered rows in the same result set.
slots.deliverable: A single table with a masking policy and a row access policy both active, confirmed by a query as a restricted role showing both effects at once.

slots.practicalActivity: Run (or write, if no live account is available) CALL SYSTEM$CLASSIFY against a test table with auto_tag set to false first, review the JSON recommendation's privacy_category and semantic_category for two columns, then run it again with auto_tag: true and write the TAG_REFERENCES_ALL_COLUMNS query that confirms the tags were actually written.
slots.deliverable: A classification run showing the recommendation-only result, the auto_tag:true result, and a confirming TAG_REFERENCES_ALL_COLUMNS query.

slots.practicalActivity: Using the classification results from the previous slot, write a report query (against TAG_REFERENCES_ALL_COLUMNS or a similar information_schema view) listing every column in your test table tagged as an IDENTIFIER or QUASI_IDENTIFIER. Then explain in one paragraph how that single tag-based report lets a governance team answer 'where is our sensitive data' across an entire database, not just one table.
slots.deliverable: A sensitive-data discovery report query plus a written explanation of how tags scale discovery beyond one table.

slots.practicalActivity: Classification lab: pick two columns from any table you've worked with in this course and classify them by hand -- is each one an IDENTIFIER or a QUASI_IDENTIFIER, and what semantic_category would SYSTEM$CLASSIFY likely assign? Then write the ALTER TAG ... SET MASKING POLICY statement wiring your Chapter 2 tag-based masking policy to a tag that would cover both columns automatically.
slots.deliverable: A manual classification of two columns with reasoning, plus one ALTER TAG statement connecting classification to enforcement.

slots.practicalActivity: Write the QUERY_HISTORY query that lists every query run in the last 24 hours with its user, role, and execution_status. Then write the ACCESS_HISTORY query using base_objects_accessed that would prove whether a query selecting from a secure view actually read a specific sensitive table behind it -- and explain in one sentence why searching the query's own text wouldn't be sufficient proof.
slots.deliverable: A working QUERY_HISTORY query and a working ACCESS_HISTORY query proving indirect access to a base table, with the text-search limitation explained.

slots.practicalActivity: Design one governance monitoring dashboard with three real tiles: a query naming the top 5 users by queries against policies_referenced (tables protected by a masking or row access policy), a query naming any Standard Edition gap if ACCESS_HISTORY is unavailable, and one tile tracking classification coverage (percentage of columns with a privacy_category tag). Name which ACCOUNT_USAGE view backs each tile.
slots.deliverable: A three-tile governance dashboard design, each tile naming its backing ACCOUNT_USAGE view and the question it answers.

slots.practicalActivity: Auditing lab: write a single ACCESS_HISTORY query that would answer a real GDPR-style data-subject request -- 'show every query and user that read the ssn column of raw_customer.customer_loyalty in the last 90 days.' Note the edition requirement (Enterprise or higher) and the latency constraint (up to 180 minutes) you'd disclose alongside the result.
slots.deliverable: A column-level ACCESS_HISTORY audit query answering a realistic compliance request, with its edition and latency caveats stated.

slots.practicalActivity: Design a Snowflake Secure Data Share for one masked table with an external business partner: name the share, confirm the masking and row access policies from Chapter 2 remain enforced for the consumer, and name a DATA_RETENTION_TIME_IN_DAYS setting you'd configure on the shared table to balance Time Travel recovery against storage cost.
slots.deliverable: A named secure data share design confirming policy enforcement for the consumer, plus a justified retention-period setting.

slots.practicalActivity: For an organization running separate dev, test, and production Snowflake accounts, name one governance control (role naming convention, masking policy, or tagging standard) that must stay identical across all three accounts to avoid a policy working in test but silently failing in production. Then complete the course's own practice lab exercise end to end, tracking which tasks you completed without looking back at earlier lessons.
slots.deliverable: One named cross-account consistency control with its failure-mode reasoning, plus a completed run of the course's practice lab.

slots.practicalActivity: Capstone review: write a one-to-two-page Snowflake data governance plan for a hypothetical company. Cover the role hierarchy and one GRANT chain, one masking policy and one row access policy protecting a real column pair, how classification (SYSTEM$CLASSIFY) and tags feed into that enforcement, an ACCESS_HISTORY query you'd run monthly to audit who touched sensitive data, and one data-sharing or retention decision for a downstream consumer.
slots.deliverable: A one-to-two-page written Snowflake governance plan covering RBAC, data protection policies, classification-driven tagging, an audit query, and one enterprise-governance decision.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: After finishing this course, a student can design a Snowflake role hierarchy and GRANT chain, write real masking and row access policies backed by mapping tables and tags, run and interpret SYSTEM$CLASSIFY to find sensitive data automatically, write ACCESS_HISTORY and QUERY_HISTORY queries that prove controls worked, and scope a governed data share across accounts -- the hands-on Snowflake governance skillset the Data Governance Engineer path assumes a student can execute, not just describe.
